The Silent Crown — Chapter 3: The Merchant's Oath

The rains came late that autumn, and the gate at Wrenshire stood open to a sky the color of old tin. Verin watched the wagons roll in, their wheels silent on the soaked cobbles, and he counted the reeds the merchants had tied to their axles. Each reed was a debt. Each debt, a promise.

"How many this season?" asked the boy at his elbow. His name was Oren, and he had followed Verin for three winters now, though no one could say why.

"Thirty-one." Verin did not look down. "And the last of them belongs to a man I trusted."

"Trust is a merchant's word," the boy muttered, "and a merchant's word is worth—"

"Careful." The old trader's voice came low and even. "You speak of my brother."

Oren went quiet. The drivers began to unload: hogsheads of salt, bales of wool, and one small iron chest that made the porters grunt when they set it down. Verin's eyes found it at once, the way a hawk finds a hare in tall grass.

"Open it," he said.

The merchant who owned the chest was a lean woman in a blue coat, and she made no move to touch the latch. "It is sealed by contract," she said, "signed in the king's name, dated the first of the month, U.S. currency, no exceptions."

Verin smiled the way old men smile at rain: not at all. "Then we shall open it in the king's name, Dr. Vane, and see what his contract has been hiding."

The iron lid rose on a silent hinge. Inside, wrapped in oilcloth and packed in sawdust, lay a crown of black glass, its points dulled as though it had been worn for a very long time.

The boy's breath caught. "That's... that isn't—"

"It is," said Verin.

And the sword moved. It hung unlit on the western wall, three feet of dark steel in a plain leather scabbard, and yet the whole room turned to it, the way a needle turns to a storm. The merchant's woman face went pale, and for the first time in his long life, Oren understood why his master had never once, in thirty years of carrying it, drawn that blade.
